Introduction

[
1
]

THE COURT:
These
are my reasons for judgment, part one. They are in respect of three of the many
issues between these parties. I will incorporate these reasons into written
reasons for judgment which will address all the issues in dispute.

[
2
]

The issues which I am addressing are whether the
parties' daughter will remain in her current school, Vancouver Talmud Torah (“VTT”),
or attend Collingwood School or another school in West Vancouver; whether Mr. Friedlander
will have final decision‑making authority in respect of the child's
education and her cultural, linguistic, religious, and spiritual upbringing and
heritage; and whether the child should have a cellphone.

[
3
]

The parties were married in August 2007, a month
before their daughter was born. They remained together as a couple until
September 2013. Throughout most of their marriage, they resided in a home in
West Vancouver, which I will refer to as Twin Creek. After they separated, Mr. Friedlander
moved to Vancouver and now resides in the area of West 14th Avenue and Oak
Street, close to VTT.

[
4
]

When the child was four, her parents registered
her in the preschool at VTT. She has now completed Grade 1 at that school.

Procedural Background

[
5
]

The notice of family claim was filed by Mr. Friedlander
on September 12, 2013. Ms. Claman filed a response on October 25, 2013,
and a counterclaim on March 31, 2014. The claimant responded to the
counterclaim on May 6, 2014.

[
6
]

The parties attended a judicial case conference
before Mr. Justice Pearlman on October 17, 2013. The only order regarding the
child was that the parties refrain from making disparaging comments about the
other while she was in their presence.

[
7
]

On November 4, 2013, Mr. Friedlander filed
an application seeking, among other things, an order that he have increased and
specified parenting time with the child. The application was heard by Master
Scarth on November 6 and 22, 2013. On the latter date, Master Scarth ordered
that the parties share interim and joint custody and be shared guardians of the
child; parenting time, including holidays, be divided equally between the
parties; each party have reasonable telephone access to the child during the
other party's parenting time; when the parent who has scheduled parenting time
is unable to care for the child, the other parent be entitled to the right of
first refusal; the parties be restrained from attending the child's school on
the other parent's parenting days, and restrained from taking the child out of
school except in emergencies.

[
8
]

Master Scarth ordered that the child continue
attending VTT until further order of the Court, and that a
Family Law Act
,
S.B.C. 2011 c. 25 s. 211 report be prepared by Dr. Rebecca St. Clere
England, with the cost to be shared equally between the parties.

Evidence

Eran Friedlander

[
9
]

Mr. Friedlander says that the child's enrolment
at VTT was a joint decision between him and Ms. Claman. A friend of Ms. Claman's,
Maureen Gales, intervened to help to get the child registered at VTT, as the
deadline for admission had passed. Mr. Friedlander says that he and Ms. Claman
always intended to send the child to VTT. They did not discuss her attending any
other school, including Collingwood School. They chose VTT because it was a
Jewish day school and they were impressed with the school and the engagement of
the entire faculty in the children’s program when they visited it. They both
thought that the teaching of Jewish culture was important. In addition, Mr. Friedlander
was born in Israel and his first language and that of his extended family is
Hebrew. That was an important feature of the decision.

[
10
]

Mr. Friedlander says when the child was in
preschool, and to some extent when she was in kindergarten, he and Ms. Claman
agreed that her attendance would not necessarily be daily. They took her out of
school for various reasons, including attendance at a ski school at Whistler
and trips to Disneyland in California. She also went to Israel with Mr. Friedlander
to see his mother, who was ill, and missed two and a half weeks of school
resulting from that trip.

[
11
]

Mr. Friedlander says he did most of the driving (80
percent) from the Twin Creek home to VTT, and when he was travelling and he was
unable to take her to school, Ms. Claman or one of her assistants would
drive her to school. Sometimes she would not go to school.

[
12
]

When the parties separated in September 2013, the
child was just beginning Grade 1 at VTT.

[
13
]

Mr. Friedlander says that he considers the
child’s attendance at school to be essential and he strives to accomplish that.
He says that he has been present for every parent‑teacher conference and
every performance and activity in which the child was involved.

[
14
]

Since September 2013, Mr. Friedlander says
he has organized playdates and sleepovers, and makes sure that the child goes
to her friends' birthday parties. He has become friendly with parents whose
children attend VTT. He has built a social network of people at VTT for the
child and for himself. He takes her and her friends to activities. He goes
himself or goes with other parents. Mr. Friedlander and the child
socialize at the Jewish community centre.

[
15
]

Mr. Friedlander says that VTT is very important
to him. He thinks it is an excellent school. He feels that things are going
well for the child at the school and that there is no need to change schools. The
level of teachers on faculty, he says, is high, and they are caring and loving.
The parents of the students are from good backgrounds. The child has been there
for three years, and Mr. Friedlander believes she is happy and safe and
has a lot of friends, and is doing well academically.

[
16
]

Mr. Friedlander says he wants his child to grow
up in a Jewish environment and pass along the values and traditions of his
parents and his and grandparents. He considers that being Jewish is more than a
religion, it is about culture and traditions, and these are handed to the child
at VT. He says the holidays at VTT are Jewish holidays, and that if the child
was at another school, she will not be able to celebrate Jewish holidays or she
will miss out on school. Mr. Friedlander says that beginning in Grade 1, the
child has studied Hebrew and she knows quite a lot of words, both in reading
and writing. He says she has acquired skills in Hebrew. He explains that her
knowledge of Hebrew is important and fosters a close relationship between her
and her paternal grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins.

[
17
]

Mr. Friedlander says in spite of his commitment
to have the child attend school on a regular basis, Ms. Claman has not
made the same commitment. The child has missed 20 days of school in Grade 1,
entirely, Mr. Friedlander says, when she is in Ms. Claman's care.

[
18
]

Mr. Friedlander also says that Ms. Claman
took the child out of school for several days after Ms. Claman's other
daughter, Mia, was hospitalized, having been shot. Mr. Friedlander objects
to her having done that on the basis that it was not the safest place for the
child and it also encroached on his parenting time.

Jody Claman

[
19
]

Ms. Claman says that she and Mr. Friedlander
discussed school for the child and agreed that she would go to Collingwood
School. She says that Mr. Friedlander was excited about the prospect. Ms. Claman
assumed that the child would be automatically accepted into Collingwood School,
as the child's half‑siblings had both attended that school. Ms. Claman
says she found out that there was not a place for the child, and when she told Mr.
Friedlander that, they were both very disappointed. She says Mr. Friedlander
blamed her, but there was nothing she could do.

[
20
]

Ms. Claman says she has lived in West Vancouver
since she was young and has a community there. The child's best friend is a
student at Collingwood School. Ms. Claman says it makes “no sense to drive
four hours every day to a program at VTT that is not instilled in [the child].”
She says, and I am quoting from my notes: "Our little girl is so
distraught. My children are my life and I have done everything so they can
enjoy their life. Everything I do is for them. If [the child] liked her school,
I would drive her. I tell her it's a great school and it's her father's
heritage."

[
21
]

Ms. Claman says the parties had no other idea,
except that the child would go to Collingwood School in West Vancouver. While Ms. Claman
agrees that VTT is, in her words, "a great little school", she says
it is not a school for the child. The child does not want to go there. The
child says she wants to go to Collingwood School. Ms. Claman says that she
feels, and I am quoting again, "that we have lied to [the child] and she
has lost trust".

[
22
]

In respect of the Hebrew language, Ms. Claman
describes all languages as great, however, she says she was raised as a
Canadian not as a Jew. She says she cannot help the child with the Hebrew
language at all.

[
23
]

In respect of Mr. Friedlander's parenting
style, Ms. Claman says that he had no experience as a husband or father. When
the child was a baby, he was not very hands‑on and had little
participation in her life. She says: "He would read to her, but she didn't
leave my side for four years... [The child] is my light, she is my love. I want
my children to be well‑adjusted and strong."

[
24
]

In respect of Mr. Friedlander having 50
percent of parenting time with the child, Ms. Claman says that he has made
bad choices for the child, including her clothing, and she has concerns about
her eating when she is with Mr. Friedlander. Ms. Claman says that Mr. Friedlander
had the child over a break, and when she came back to Ms. Claman's home, the
child was sick and had lost a significant amount of weight.

[
25
]

Ms. Claman justifies her decision to keep the
child out of school and away from Mr. Friedlander in the period following
her daughter's shooting. She says that the child stayed with her friend, Ms. Gales,
and that she wanted to keep the child out of the public eye. Ms. Claman
agrees that she took the child out for dinner on one of the nights following
the shooting that was during Mr. Friedlander's parenting time.

[
26
]

Ms. Claman says that in the summer of 2013, Mr. Friedlander
had a "drug‑induced stroke". Ms. Claman says she wanted to
make sure that the child had a cellphone so she could call 911. Ms. Claman's
friend, Michele Florian, bought the child a cellphone. Ms. Claman says she
wishes to speak to the child every night when she is in Mr. Friedlander's
care. She says, "I build my night around it and [the child] looks forward
to it. I worry that something might happen to Mr. Friedlander."

[
27
]

Ms. Florian also paid the cost of having the
child assessed for Collingwood School and the deposit for her place at the
school. Ms. Claman says that if the child goes to VTT, that she is
committed to Collingwood School for just under $20,000. She says, and I am
quoting, "I understand that I promised [the child] and I keep my bargain,
unlike others. Therefore, I will pay for it and I will work to pay it off to Ms. Florian."

[
28
]

Ms. Claman says that she did not apply to
Collingwood School for the child in 2011 or 2012. Before the separation in
2013, she agrees that she did not make any application for the child to go to
Collingwood School or to be assessed. She raised the assessment with Mr. Friedlander
after the parties separated.

[
29
]

Ms. Claman does not remember if she told Mr. Friedlander
that she wanted the child to go to Collingwood School. She recalls telling him
she got a bill from VTT in the fall of 2013 that she asked him to pay, and she
told Mr. Friedlander that if he did not pay that bill, she would make
other arrangements for the child's education.

[
30
]

Ms. Claman says that she is aware that the Court
has not decided where the child will attend Grade 2 and continuing. She is
aware of communication from Mr. Friedlander's lawyer that she is not to
discuss going to Collingwood School with the child. She says, "I did
anyway. I don't lie to my children."

[
31
]

Ms. Claman says her friend, Michele Florian,
loaned her $300,000 to pay for Ms. Claman's legal fees and enable Ms. Claman
to be, in Ms. Claman's words, "[the child’s] voice".

[
32
]

Ms. Claman says that she sees pictures of the
child with other children at VTT. She describes them as fabricated scenarios on
Mother's Day, when the child was with other children and was smiling. Ms. Claman
says that Mr. Friedlander outsources the child. A lot of the times she has
seen the child with friends of the claimant's, but they are new friends. Ms. Claman
says she has a "huge issue" with the child being with her friend and
her friend’s mother who were involved in the “sweater incident”, which I will
discuss below. She says there are also inappropriate people that Mr. Friedlander
has left the child with, describing one as "Patrick with porno on the
website".

[
33
]

Ms. Claman made other allegations about Mr. Friedlander
and his parenting abilities and she agreed were sometimes made in the child's
presence. For instance, she has alleged that he does not look after the child
properly and is incapable of doing so. He does not support the child
financially. The child goes to school sick when she is in his care. He drives the
child to school when he is drunk. He poses a flight risk if allowed to travel
internationally with the child. He has hit the child in the face with his iPad.
He told the child that Jews are chosen people. He is a criminal. He sexually
abuses the child. His father and brother are criminals. The child is afraid of Mr. Friedlander's
mother. Mr. Friedlander's sister is a thief. Mr. Friedlander stole
items from Twin Creek belonging to Ms. Claman. She also alleged in her
evidence that Mr. Friedlander has gangland ties and does business with
known gang members.

Evidence Regarding VTT

[
34
]

Cathy Lowenstein is the head of school for VTT
and has been for 11 years. She describes VTT as an independent, faith‑based
school. It has the same learning outcomes as public schools, as well as being a
Jewish day school, and a pluralistic community school. She says that VTT offers
half a day of Judaic studies, in addition to the regular curriculum, which VTT
follows but in a shorter time.

[
35
]

Ms. Lowenstein says that there is diversity
among the students and parents at the school. Some are not religious; others
are very observant. One parent must be Jewish in order to enrol a child in VTT.
The families do not need to be affiliated with a synagogue. The school has 510
students who attend a large compound on Oak Street and King Edward Avenue in
Vancouver. The children are brought to school by their parents. They do not
normally walk to school, because they come from all over the city, including
North and West Vancouver.

[
36
]

Families start their children at VTT at
preschool. Ms. Lowenstein says that VTT has very low attrition rates. Families
make a decision early on in a child's school life, and once the students start
kindergarten, the students generally go to Grade 7.

[
37
]

At the conclusion of the VTT program, students
will be fluent in English and Hebrew, and will have a working knowledge of
French. They start a Hebrew language program in Grade 1. Ms. Lowenstein
says it is important for the children to be at school every day, because the
curriculum is fast paced, and to be away for even a half a day is a problem for
a student.

[
38
]

In respect of the child at school, Ms. Lowenstein
says she is a beautiful child, inside and out, and is very happy to be in the
school. She skips down the hall. She is a keen learner who does very well. She
loves Hebrew. She has a great relationship with the teachers, and she is a
joyful learner. The child has many friends at school. Ms. Lowenstein sees
her in the hallways and playground with her friends.

[
39
]

Ms. Lowenstein says the school does not promote
clannishness or exclusivity, nor is it engaged in forced indoctrination. There
are some Israelis at the school, but they represent a small percentage. Some of
the Israeli students are in Vancouver for a couple of years and then return to
Israel; some live here permanently and remain at the school. Parents choose VTT
as the school for their children because they want to have their children
exposed to the rich traditions of Judaism.

[
40
]

Ms. Lowenstein says she has never heard that
teachers do not like Ms. Claman. She has never heard the child comment
about not liking the school. She sees the child's face when she comes in the
morning to school and she is smiling and happy, and she is involved in all
programs available.

[
41
]

Ms. Lowenstein says that VTT is a community‑based
school and has a diverse population. Teachers and parents support the students
to make sure that it is a gathering place for the family, and VTT excels
academically.

[
42
]

The school follows the Jewish calendar, and has
days off for holidays on Jewish holidays.

[
43
]

Ms. Lowenstein explains that VTT has only one
point of entry and exit, the front door. The school and the playground are self‑enclosed.
There is no exit from the playground. There is a security guard at the front
door, although there have been no incidents at VTT. If a person not connected
to a child wishes entry, he or she must first buzz at the front door. The
second set of doors is locked and it is only unlocked if the person identifies
him or herself and the purpose of the visit.

[
44
]

Ms. Lowenstein said she was not contacted by Dr. England
and did not provide any description of the school or its programs.

[
45
]

Janet Lisa Kaplan and Orly Gal are the child's
teachers. Ms. Kaplan teaches in the English program, Ms. Gal in the
Hebrew program.

[
46
]

Ms. Kaplan says that she is satisfied with how the
child is doing at school. She says she is at grade level and makes wonderful
progress. Ms. Kaplan has not heard the child say that she does not like
the school or she does not have any friends. There are no concerns about the
child at the school, academically or socially. She is not aware of any teacher
not liking Ms. Claman. Ms. Kaplan says she cares for the child very
much, as the other teachers do.

[
47
]

Ms. Gal describes the child as very happy and
well‑adjusted, that she participates in all activities, that she is a
good student and that she has quite a few friends. She also says she cares
about the child, as the other teachers and staff at VTT do. The child has not
suggested to Ms. Gal that she does not like Hebrew or that she does not
like the school and is not happy there.

The “sweater incident”

[
48
]

In mid‑November 2013, an incident occurred
between the child and a fellow student, who I will refer to as “the friend”. Mr. Friedlander
says that the friend lent the child a sweater and that he gave the sweater back
to the friend's mother the following day. The child showed up for school in a
different sweater the next day.

[
49
]

Ms. Gal advised both of the child's parents of
the sweater incident, stating:

We had a little
confusion today between [the friend] and [the child] that led to tears for both
parties. [The child] had a sweater that she was wearing in the beginning of
recess, and [the friend] insisted that the sweater belonged to her and tried to
take it back. Both Ms. Kaplan and I tried to figure out exactly what
happened, and as far as we can understand, there has been an arrangement
between the parents and the sweater belonged to [the child]. The girls made
peace and all ends well.

[
50
]

Ms. Kaplan says that the event was a
misunderstanding, and after the friend apologized to the child, the day
continued as normal. The child continues to be friends with that friend and the
other girls. The friend's mother describes the event as being her fault. She
did not tell her daughter that the sweater had been returned to her by Mr. Friedlander.
The friend’s mother says that she and her daughter apologized to the child, and
that that was the end of it.

[
51
]

Ms. Claman's response to the teachers about the
sweater incident was described in an email that she sent to VTT the following
day, after she received Ms. Gal's email. She described the event as:
"Bullying at the utmost!" Ms. Claman continues, "I want
answers and discipline!  People must be aware of physical bullying that is
going on with six‑year‑old students."

[
52
]

Neither Ms. Gal nor Ms. Kaplan
described the event as bullying.

[
53
]

In her evidence, Ms. Claman says that when the
child came home from school on November 18, 2013, she told her mother what had
occurred in regard to the sweater incident. Ms. Claman told the child that
she must forgive and move forward, and that that would be the appropriate way
to handle it. She wrote the email that I have quoted the following day. The
child now adopts the bullying interpretation of the event.

Dr. England

[
54
]

Dr. England prepared her
s. 211
report,
Psychological Evaluation in the matter of Eran Friedlander and Jody Claman,
dated May 20, 2014. The report was prepared to address the matter of joint
custody and shared parenting on a permanent basis. Dr. England also made a
recommendation regarding the school that the child should attend. Dr. England
interviewed Mr. Friedlander and Ms. Claman and conducted
psychological testing of both. She interviewed the child and she interviewed
collaterals suggested by Mr. Friedlander and Ms. Claman.

[
55
]

Dr. England begins by describing Ms. Claman's
self‑report. She describes her as a very successful businesswoman and
being treated by wealthy friends. Dr. England asked Ms. Claman if she
had any plans to relocate out of West Vancouver, to which Ms. Claman
responded, "if an opportunity came my way ‑ I'm willing to go
anywhere" and if she was offered work somewhere for four months, she would
go. She said that she would take the child with her, adding "it's all
about [the child]".

[
56
]

In respect of her relationship with Mr. Friedlander,
Ms. Claman told Dr. England that it was a horribly abusive marriage. Ms. Claman
told Dr. England that Mr. Friedlander was a heavy pot smoker and
would smoke daily, morning and night. Ms. Claman suggested to Dr. England
that this led to Mr. Friedlander's irritability which has been directed at
the child. Ms. Claman suggested that Mr. Friedlander may be bisexual.
She describes his moods as horrendous and his morose behaviour as shocking. She
told Dr. England that she and Mr. Friedlander had stopped sleeping
together, although Mr. Friedlander continued to sleep with the child.

[
57
]

Ms. Claman expressed to Dr. England that
the joint parenting that was ordered by Master Scarth was:

. . .
cut[ting] my six year old in half. Giving a man a six year old little girl and
putting her in danger. I honestly feel this is a terrible form of child abuse.
Something has to be done to protect Mothers & Children from such abuse. The
only person who suffers in the end is THE CHILD and that is not in Child's Best
Interest. This is Canada. We live in a country of Democracy.

[
58
]

Ms. Claman also described the child's experience
at VTT to Dr. England. She told Dr. England that the child was doing okay,
but did not have the opportunity to build friendships.

[
59
]

Ms. Claman told Dr. England that the
child was underweight and that was one of her concerns about Mr. Friedlander's
parenting. She says Mr. Friedlander is moody; if the child disagrees with
him, he screams at her. She is concerned that the child just goes along with
what her father wants.

[
60
]

Ms. Claman described Mr. Friedlander as
being on serious depression drugs and threatening to kill himself many times
when they were together. Ms. Claman told Dr. England that Mr. Friedlander
is inattentive to the child's basic physical care and the child has been
returned to her sick. The child reports to her mother of not being fed while in
Mr. Friedlander's care. Ms. Claman described to Dr. England the
child being returned to her with matted hair, filthy fingernails, and never
having the correct shoes or boots on. She is concerned that Mr. Friedlander
is still sleeping with the child at his home.

[
61
]

In respect of attending VTT, Dr. England
describes what Ms. Claman told her:

Ms. Claman
objects to [the child] attending [VTT]. Noting that Mr. Friedlander is an
"Israeli Jew" which is "different than American Jews" she
said "I'm not a religious Jew" and is concerned that [the child] is
undergoing "forced indoctrination" that will set her apart from
others. She stated that when Mr. Friedlander drank "he became so cruel
towards other races of people, especially Muslims."  Mr. Friedlander
"would always tell [the child] she was the chosen people" whereas Ms.
Claman would tell her "we are all God's children."  She said "I
don't believe in clannishness and exclusivity, which is promoted in VTT. Only
Jews can attend the school - mainly Israeli's" and she does not want [the
child] educated in a religious school. She noted that both her son and daughter
attended Collingwood in West Vancouver, and yet had Bars and Bat Mitzvah
ceremonies in keeping with their Jewish heritage, while at the same time
celebrating Christmas.

[
62
]

Dr. England asked Ms. Claman some
additional questions and describes her responses as follows:

Ms. Claman was asked some additional
questions arising from concerns expressed by Mr. Friedlander. She denied that
she speaks badly about Mr. Friedlander to [the child]. When asked more about
her communications with [the child], she said she told [the child]
"Dr. Rebecca, she will tell the judge what you want, you get to choose,
make sure you express everything" adding "I think [the child's] voice
should be heard."

…

When asked about [the child's] school, Ms.
Claman said she was initially going to go to Collingwood in West
Vancouver, but they missed the deadline for application. Assisted by Ms.
Claman's friend Maureen, [the child] was able to start school at VTT, with the
plan being to change to Collingwood once there was an opening. Ms. Claman said
the teachers at VTT don't like her because "I'm not Israeli" adding
somewhat pejoratively "they're in Birkenstocks."

…

Taking all of
the above into account, Ms. Claman believes that it would be best for [the
child] to be based in West Vancouver, attend a non-denominational school, and
live primarily with her. [Ms. Claman] felt it would be best "not to over
stress Eran with daily duties" and suggested that he have [the child]
"every other weekend" in addition to having two mid week visits from
after school until after dinner.

[
63
]

Dr. England conducted a number of personality
tests on each party.

[
64
]

The results of Ms. Claman's personality
tests showed her defensiveness as higher than 99 percent of people involved in
custody litigation and that she has narcissistic tendencies. Dr. England
says that there was some element of more than five of the nine criteria on the
Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition, (DSM‑5)
to a significant enough degree to support that Ms. Claman has a
narcissistic personality disorder. Dr. England also noted marked
elevations on other indicators, tending to suggest self‑favourable
presentation and conscious distortion.

[
65
]

She says Ms. Claman's grandiosity score on
the Personality Assessment Inventory testing demonstrates that Ms. Claman
is difficult to communicate and to co-parent with on matters regarding the
child.

[
66
]

Mr. Friedlander's results were less pronounced,
with his defensiveness being of little significance when compared to the
normative data. In respect of her assessment of Eran Friedlander, Dr. England
says that he denies any substance abuse history. He has a moderate habitual use
of alcohol, two glasses of wine twice a week. He said that he smoked marihuana
regularly, that is, once a week, from his mid‑twenties, including when he
was with Ms. Claman, but stopped two years ago.

[
67
]

In regard to how the child is doing at VTT, Mr. Friedlander
told Dr. England that she was excelling academically and had lots of good
friends, and teachers who support and love her. Mr. Friedlander expressed
concern that the child was being impacted by the situation between her parents,

Legal Framework

[
100
]

The legal framework is set out in the
Divorce
Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.) and the
Family Law Act
. Their
interplay was explained in the decision of Madam Justice Humphries in
Hansen
v. Mantei-Hansen
,
2013 BCSC 876
. I will not go through that decision in
this oral judgment.
Hansen
and subsequent decisions have made it
abundantly clear that the court must consider only the best interests of the
child, in particular those enumerated in s. 37(2). Those that are relevant
here are:

(a) the child's health and emotional
well-being;

(b) the child's views, unless it would be
inappropriate to consider them;

(c) the nature and strength of the
relationships between the child and significant persons in the child's life;

(d) the history of the child's care;

(e) the child's need for stability, given
the child's age and stage of development;

(f) the ability of each person who is a
guardian or seeks guardianship of the child, or who has or seeks parental
responsibilities, parenting time or contact with the child, to exercise his or
her responsibilities;

…

(i) the appropriateness of an arrangement
that would require the child's guardians to cooperate on issues affecting the
child, including whether requiring cooperation would increase any risks to the
safety, security or well-being of the child or other family members;

(j) any civil or
criminal proceeding relevant to the child's safety, security or well-being.

[
101
]

Section 37(3) provides that:

. . .
[an] order is not in the best interests of a child unless it protects, to the
greatest extent possible, the child's physical, psychological and emotional
safety, security and well-being.

102

s. 41

of the
Family Law Act
provides, and I will just refer to those relevant

(d) making decisions respecting the child's
education and participation in extracurricular activities, including the
nature, extent and location;

(e) making decisions respecting the child's
cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual upbringing and heritage . . .

. . .

(l) exercising
any other responsibilities reasonably necessary to nurture the child's
development.

[

evidence. He was critical of Ms. Claman for making accusations about him,
such as those I described, for example, that he is a criminal or a drunk or a
drug taker, and he was critical of her for suggesting that he was not a fit
parent and for casting aspersions on him in front of the child. Ms. Claman
said the same negative things about him in her evidence, but provided nothing

was an excellent father. This is absolutely contrary to the evidence that she
gave in Court.

[
107
]

I found Ms. Claman to exaggerate, to embellish, and to avoid
answering questions. Her evidence was internally inconsistent and inconsistent
with what she stated in examination for discovery or in affidavits filed with

said was true, although that did not appear to be her position when she gave

[

]

[

]

I am further convinced that Ms. Claman will say anything she

the school was that it was a religious school and that though both she and Mr. Friedlander
are Jewish, Mr. Friedlander was much more religious than Ms. Claman. That,
too, is not borne out by the evidence, although I accept that his commitment to
Jewish heritage and traditions may be somewhat greater than that of Ms. Claman.

[

Jew. His desire to have the child attend VTT is so she will be exposed to
Jewish traditions and so she will be able to speak Hebrew, his first language
and the language of his family. Dr. England did not appear to consider
that those factors were important.

[
124
]

More importantly, though, is that the religiosity of VTT does not
appear to be Ms. Claman's objection to the school, based on the evidence
she provided. She expressed that VTT is a great little school, but not for the
child, and that it is pointless to drive her there, she says consuming four
hours in traffic.

[

]

school would be a neutral factor. I do not find on the evidence that Ms. Claman
has a great objection to the child attending a Jewish school or a religious
school; it is its location to which she objects. This is an area where I find
that Ms. Claman attempted to manipulate Dr. England.

[
126
]

and I will address it as a second issue, but as I have noted, it is the most
important, and likely the only, issue for Ms. Claman. Dr. England
suggests that it would be best if Mr. Friedlander moved to West Vancouver
and the child attended school there. Perhaps that is so, but I cannot order Mr. Friedlander
to move to West Vancouver. I am satisfied that he moved to Vancouver for the
appropriate reasons, including to be close to the school that the parties had
agreed that the child would attend, and he is promoting the child's best
interests by assisting her with playdates and becoming friends with other
parents at the school.

[
127
]

child's uncanny alignment with Ms. Claman's view, was persuaded to a
significant degree by what the child said about the school. She found them
corroborative of Ms. Claman's view of VTT. Given what the child had to say
to her about VTT, Dr. England appears to accept the child's view that she
is not happy there and that she really wished to attend Collingwood School, the
school of her choice.

[
128
]

Dr. England did not know that in her argument, Ms. Claman would
abandon her position that the child's views should be considered. Dr. England
was not examined about what difference that may make in her recommendations,
because it was not known to Mr. Friedlander's counsel at the time the
examination took place. I find that had Dr. England known that, she would
have considered that to be significant and that it may have given her reason to
reconsider her recommendation about VTT and Collingwood School.

[

]

would neutralize the conflict between her parents. The issue of where the child
goes to school is critically important and divisive, but I cannot find that it
will lessen the conflict between these parties significantly. As Dr. England
noted in her evidence, Ms. Claman is responsible for the conflict about
the school, and it is not certain that acceding to Ms. Claman's view will
prevent further conflict. Dr. England observes that a change at this stage
of the child's educational course and school will not create the disruption and
instability that it would in an older child. This not a reason to support a
change of school at this time. I must consider the impact on the child
presently.

Section 37 factors

[
130
]

Applying the relevant factors stated in s. 37(2), I find that the
child’s best interest will be served by continuing her schooling at VTT:

(a)

The child’s health and emotional well‑being:
I accept the evidence of the witnesses who observed the child and have observed
her for three years at VTT. She is happy, a joyous learner, she has many
friends, and she is an active participant in school activities. Indeed, it is
the one place where she does not have to think about the conflicts between her
parents and how she will negotiate between them.

(b)

The child's views, unless it would be
inappropriate to consider them:  the parties agree that I should not consider the
child's views as expressed to Dr. England. In that regard, I will not
consider them, nor will I consider the child's views that Ms. Claman says
that the child has expressed to her.

(c)

The nature and strength of the relationships
between the child and significant persons in the child's life: I accept that the
child is significantly bonded to both her parents, her father's extended family
and, to some extent, her mother's, and to Ms. Claman's friends.

(d)

The history of the child's care: both parties
have contributed to the child's care throughout her life. In respect of school
care, she has received that through VTT throughout her entire educational
career.

(e)

The child's need for stability, given the
child's age and stage of development: I find that a move to a different school
will impact the child's stability at this age and stage. While it may be of
less impact if she is moved now, it cannot be said that it will not affect her
stability. It is not a factor that supports a move to Collingwood School.

(f)

The ability of each person who is a guardian…or who has or
seeks parental responsibilities and parenting time with the child, to
exercise his or her responsibilities: I have expressed my views about Ms. Claman
and her attempts to manipulate the child. It is of grave concern. However, I
accept that the parties have agreed to joint parenting and Dr. England's
recommendation in that regard.

(i)      The appropriateness of an arrangement that would require
the child's guardians to cooperate on issues affecting the child, including
whether requiring cooperation would increase any risks to the safety, security
or well-being of the child or other family members: I will address this matter
further when I consider Mr. Friedlander's request to have sole parenting
responsibilities in respect of the child's education and religion.

(j)      Any civil or criminal proceeding relevant to the child's
safety, security or well-being: while this factor is not strictly applicable, I
consider that VTT assures that the child is safe and secure and that it is the
best place for her, particularly in light of the events involving her half‑sister.

[
131
]

Section 37(3) provides:

. . .
[an] order is not in the best interests of a child unless it protects, to the
greatest extent possible, the child's physical, psychological and emotional
safety, security and well-being.

[
132
]

The child has attended VTT for three years. She has formed friendships
there. As I have said, the witnesses who gave evidence about the child at VTT
say she is happy and doing well. Her physical, psychological and emotional
safety, security and well‑being are well served by VTT. I have no
evidence upon which to reach any conclusion about how the child's best
interests would be served at Collingwood School or any other school.

[
133
]

I therefore order that the child continue her elementary schooling
at VTT.

of Ms. Claman's hands. I have found her to be manipulative, and I expect that
